No Result View All Result Home News Politics Business Sport Football Health Entertainment Education Opinion Editorial Columns Others LeVogue Magazine Conferences National Economy Contact Us Hausa Edition Home News Politics Business Sport Football Health Entertainment Education Opinion Editorial Columns Others LeVogue Magazine Conferences National Economy Contact Us No Result View All Result No Result View All Result At UK Varsity, NILDS DG Sulaiman Advocates People-centred, Results-driven Leadership by James Kwen 1 minute ago in Politics Share on WhatsApp Share on Facebook Share on X Telegram The Director-General of the National Institute for Legislative and Democratic Studies (NILDS), Professor Abubakar Sulaiman, has called for purposeful, people-centred and results-driven leadership, declaring that the true measure of leadership lies not in the authority an individual wields but in the strength of the institutions they leave behind.
Sulaiman made this assertion while delivering a keynote address titled “Leadership in Practice: Making Decisions, Managing People and Delivering Results” at the International Leadership Summit held at the University of Brighton, United Kingdom.
Addressing an international gathering of leaders, thinkers and changemakers, the Director-General drew on more than three decades of experience spanning academia and public service to highlight the principles that distinguish effective leadership from the mere occupation of public office.
“Leadership is not the privilege of those who occupy high office; it is the discipline of those who accept responsibility for changing the trajectory of institutions and improving the lives of people. Titles confer authority, but only character, competence and vision confer leadership,” he declared.
Sulaiman identified three enduring pillars of leadership in practice: making sound decisions, managing people with different expectations, and delivering measurable results.
According to him, contemporary institutions require leaders who can navigate uncertainty, cultivate human potential and translate vision into tangible public value.
Using NILDS as a practical case study, Sulaiman demonstrated how deliberate leadership, institutional resolve and strategic execution can reposition public institutions for greater relevance and impact.
He recounted the Institute’s evolution under his leadership, highlighting its expansion from four operational departments to thirteen professionalised departments, the establishment of new institutional centres and Democracy Radio, and the strengthening of its research, legislative drafting, academic and capacity-building functions.
Sulaiman also reflected on the completion of NILDS’ permanent complex, describing the milestone as more than an infrastructural achievement. Following years of delay, the Institute moved into its ultra-modern permanent complex on 25 May 2023, marking a significant chapter in its institutional development.
“That relocation was much more than a physical movement. It represented institutional stability, growth, identity and a long-term vision for democratic capacity-building,” he stated.
Sulaiman emphasised that meaningful institutional transformation requires leaders to confront difficult challenges rather than become accustomed to longstanding limitations.
“Leadership, at its core, requires the courage to confront what is difficult rather than simply manage what is convenient,”he said.
The NILDS Director-General stressed that sustainable institutional growth depends on recognising the value of human capital, embracing diverse perspectives and creating an environment in which individuals can contribute meaningfully to a shared purpose.
“If decision-making is the heart of leadership, managing people is its soul. No leader achieves anything alone,” he said.
Emphasising that leadership must be judged by outcomes rather than intentions, Sulaiman outlined key institutional achievements recorded at NILDS over the past seven years.
These include the delivery of more than 200 capacity-building programmes, the training of over 3,000 legislators, parliamentary staff and public officials, the establishment of more than 20 strategic partnerships, and strengthened legislative capacity across Nigeria’s 36 State Houses of Assembly.
He also underscored the importance of youth inclusion, citing the Institute’s internship opportunities for young lawyers in legislative drafting and its annual engagement of over 60 National Youth Service Corps members.
“Vision without execution is fantasy. Decisions without outcomes are intentions. Managing people without results is merely activity. Leadership must translate vision into measurable impact,” he declared.
Sulaiman further observed that the ultimate value of institutional achievements lies in the capacity they create for future generations, positioning NILDS as an emerging African democratic knowledge hub where legislative research, executive education, parliamentary diplomacy and democratic innovation converge.
He urged leaders to anchor decisions in purpose rather than popularity, value people before processes, and measure results by the strength of the institutions they leave behind.
Sulaiman maintained that leadership in a rapidly changing world requires evidence-based decision-making, people-centred management and results-oriented execution, regardless of geographical or political context.
“Leadership is a practice, not a position,” he affirmed, adding that institutional transformation occurs when leaders develop the courage, vision and resilience to confront challenges, even under unfavourable circumstances.
“History rarely remembers those who merely occupied office. It remembers those who expanded the possibilities of institutions, elevated the dignity of people and left society more capable than they found it.”
He concluded by calling for a generation of leaders committed to strengthening democratic institutions, elevating human dignity and bequeathing a more capable society to those who follow.
“That, to me, is the essence of leadership in practice. It is the leadership Africa deserves. It is the leadership democratic institutions require. And it is the leadership this generation must be prepared to bequeath to the next,” Sulaiman said.
